A small dog. A young woman who lost one of hers. Something is beginning on Market Street, and I didn't plan any of it.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c092cd5c80cc7ef09d9860", "tabs": [ "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c0930345fcea86fbc5577d", "69c0a0d2dad175912e825b7b", "69c22206c7ede1d4fc6a5fa1", "69ceb106e494594cb3ad487d", "69ceb10ad5f08e5f266cd156" ], "main-content": "

Market Street moves fast. Tech workers, tourists, a man with a shopping cart, a woman on the phone — the sidewalk does not slow for anyone. I was heading home through downtown San Francisco after an appointment when the craving hit: chocolate and caramel. I had Remy with me, my small dog, and I stepped into the candy store. I did not know I was beginning something.

Most of my life, caring about other people felt like a task I was supposed to perform. Every conversation carried pressure I had not asked for — the low hum of expectation, the guilt when I let a moment pass. I moved through encounters scanning for the opening, half-present, half-performing. San Francisco quietly dismantled that.

You cannot walk Market Street distracted and actually see it. The city asks too much of you. The unhoused man two doors down from the candy store. The young woman behind the counter. The dog that everyone stops for. If you are not paying attention, you miss all of it.

That first visit, a young woman put my order together. Her attention moved immediately to Remy. Her whole demeanor shifted — the kind that happens only when someone genuinely loves dogs. She did. She owned one. The conversation lasted a minute, ordinary by any measure. Nothing stood out.

The following week I walked back down Market Street, this time buying for Debby rather than for myself. The same young woman was working. When my turn came, I mentioned I had been in the week before, with my dog. Her eyes went blank. I added the detail: small dog, black and brown markings, eyes that move around a room like he is already planning something. Something came back. She remembered Remy.

I asked how her dog was doing.

That question opened something. She had recently lost one of her dogs — a dog that weighed only eight pounds. But she told me about him with pride. He had been trained as a service dog, specifically for her. She once had epileptic seizures, and this dog had watched over her. Dogs can detect changes before they happen. If she was seizing, he would alert her parents.

We talked longer than we should have, given that she was working. I kept asking questions. She kept answering. When I finally turned to leave, I heard her voice behind me.

See you next week. She said it with a wide smile.

I walked home down Howard Street thinking about Oracle Park. Years ago, a comment like that at the ballpark marked the start of five years of conversations I never planned — the kind that went deeper than either of us expected, season after season. Something about that city block, that ballpark, that regular presence.

Is it happening again?

What I keep learning is that the people I pass every day in downtown San Francisco are not waiting for someone to arrive with something to offer them. They are already in the middle of their own stories. Janie's story — the dog, the seizures, the eight pounds of loyal animal that watched over her — was already there, fully formed, before I ever walked in. I did not bring it. I just asked one more question.

Each encounter is not an opportunity for me to do something. It is a chance to see what Jesus is already doing in someone else.

That shift makes the whole thing different. Lighter, even. Jesus is the primary actor. I am just paying attention to what He is already doing.

What would you notice tomorrow if you walked your regular route a little more slowly? Not as a practice. Not as a resolution. Just — what is already happening in the people around you that you have not asked about yet?

Janie is working again next week. Remy may or may not be with me. But I will be paying attention.
